fr.considerations: Single Access Point; Long Driveway; Dense Vegetation; Open Terrain; Limited Rear Access
fr.recommendations: Ensuring that the single access point and extended driveway remain clear of obstructions at all times could significantly improve emergency vehicle approach and reduce response delays. Maintaining adequate driveway width and surface conditions along the full length of the approach would support heavier emergency apparatus maneuvering. Clearly marking the primary access point from the main road may assist responding units in locating the entry quickly, particularly under low-visibility conditions. Where the unpaved trail extends toward the rear of the property, keeping that route passable could provide an alternate path for responder movement and staging, partially offsetting the limited rear access identified on the property.

wildfire.conditions: Scattered Shrubs; Continuous Shrub Cover; Heavy Brush; Brush Concentration; Scattered Shrubs; Mixed Vegetation Cover; Open Terrain; Fuel Continuity; Vegetated Access Route; Single Access Route; Wildland Interface; Brushland Interface
wildfire.recommendations: Reducing fuel continuity within the shrub and brush concentrations on the property, particularly where heavy brush and continuous shrub cover exist, could improve defensible space around the structure and reduce opportunities for fire to move through the landscape. Where scattered shrubs transition into denser brush concentrations, increasing separation between vegetation clusters may further reduce fuel continuity and support suppression operations. The single access route serving the property warrants attention, as maintaining vegetation clearance along both sides of the driveway or access road could improve firefighter access and support evacuation. Managing vegetation height and density along the access corridor would help preserve visibility and passability under adverse conditions. The open terrain areas on the property represent a natural fuel break that is worth preserving by limiting encroachment from adjacent brush and mixed vegetation. Continued vegetation management near any structures or improvements at the wildland interface could meaningfully reduce structure exposure and support long-term wildfire resilience.
